title: Grade 4 SOCIAL STUDIES — 2.1 Inter-dependence of people

pages.lesson:
PAGE 1: Overview

OVERVIEW
========

Interdependence means that people need one another. In your county, families depend on farmers and traders for food, on hospitals when they are sick, and on places of worship and neighbours for support. This sub-strand shows those links, the benefits they bring, and how to present them on a chart, in a role-play and in a poem.

## Strand 2.0: People and Population
Sub-strand 2.1: Inter-dependence of people
Suggested lessons: 6

## Learning outcomes
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) identify ways in which people depend on each other in the county
b) explain the benefits of interdependence of people in the county
c) use chart to illustrate the benefits of interdependence people
d) appreciate the interdependence of people in the County

## What this sub-strand covers
• trade
• farming
• hospital
• worship places

## Key inquiry questions
1. How do people in the county depend on each other?
2. Why should we support each other in the county?

## Core competencies
• Citizenship: Learners explain the benefits of interdependence of people in the county.
• Creativity and imagination: Learners role-play the interdependence of people in the county.

## Values
• Social justice: Learners discuss benefits of interdependence among people in the county

## Pertinent and contemporary issues
• Social cohesion: Learners identify ways in which people depend on each other in the county.
• Social cohesion: Learners respect others’ views/feelings as they work to create a chart on benefits of interdependence among people.

## Links to other learning areas
• English: Learners develop communication skills as they recite a poem about the importance of interdependence of people.
• Religious Education: Learners explain the importance of interdependence.

## Source
• KICD Grade 4 Social Studies Curriculum Design (Revised 2024) — Strand 2.0 People and Population, Sub-strand 2.1 Inter-dependence of people

PAGE 2: Lesson 1: People need one another

LESSON 1: PEOPLE NEED ONE ANOTHER
=================================

## What you will learn
• Explain the meaning of interdependence.
• Identify examples of people depending on each other in the county.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify ways in which people depend on each other in the county

## Introduction
Think about your breakfast. Someone grew the food, someone may have sold it, and someone at home cooked it. You depended on those people before the day even started.

## Notes
To depend on someone is to need them for something you cannot easily do alone. Interdependence means the need goes both ways. You need the farmer, and the farmer needs buyers so that the family can get money for soap, school costs and tools.

Nobody in a county grows all their own food, treats every illness, builds every house and teaches every child. People specialise. One person farms, another treats the sick, another teaches, another sells goods, another drives a vehicle. Specialising works only because people depend on each other.

### Examples close to you
Walk through one day and name the people you need:

- At home, you depend on the people who care for you. They depend on you to do your chores and to tell the truth.
- At school, you depend on your teachers. Teachers depend on learners to come ready to learn, and on parents to support the school.
- On the road, you depend on drivers to watch for walkers. Drivers depend on walkers to cross carefully.
- In the market, buyers and sellers depend on each other.

### In the county
The same pattern is larger. Villages depend on towns for some goods and services. Towns depend on villages for food. Neighbouring counties may trade with yours. When a hospital in one sub-county serves families from another, those families and that hospital are interdependent.

Brainstorm a list under the heading "People we need in our county". Keep the list for the next lessons, which look closely at trade, farming, hospitals and places of worship. Those four are important ways interdependence shows itself, but they are not the only ways.

A person who says "I need nobody" still uses roads others built, food others grew and a language others taught. Seeing the links is the first step to appreciating them.

## Key words
• depend — to need someone or something
• interdependence — people needing one another, so that each person both gives and receives help
• specialise — to do one kind of work that others rely on

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A tailor sews uniforms and buys maize from a farmer. Who depends on whom?

Working:
1. The farmer needs the tailor's payment, which comes because people need uniforms.
2. The tailor needs the farmer's maize for food.

Answer: They depend on each other. The tailor needs food, and the farmer needs buyers.

## Activity: Brainstorm who we need
You will need: Manila paper, Marker pens
1. In groups, brainstorm ways people in the county depend on each other.
2. Write each idea as "The ___ depends on the ___ for ___."
3. Read the list to the class and add ideas from other groups.
4. Underline any examples about trade, farming, a hospital or a place of worship.

## Practice
1. What does interdependence mean?
2. Give one way learners and teachers depend on each other.
3. Why does specialising make interdependence necessary?

## Summary
• Interdependence means people need one another.
• A single day shows many people you depend on.
• Trade, farming, hospitals and places of worship are important examples in the county.

### Answers to practice
1. People need one another, so that each person both gives help and receives help.
2. Learners need teachers to learn, and teachers need learners to come ready to learn.
3. When each person does one kind of work, they must rely on other people for the rest of what they need.

PAGE 3: Lesson 2: Trade and farming

LESSON 2: TRADE AND FARMING
===========================

## What you will learn
• Describe how farmers, traders and buyers depend on one another.
• Trace one food from the farm to the home.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify ways in which people depend on each other in the county

## Introduction
A market day is a picture of interdependence. Sacks of grain, vegetables, fish or milk arrive because farmers and traders need the people who have come to buy.

## Notes
Trade is the buying and selling of goods and services. Farming is the growing of crops and the keeping of animals. The two activities lock together.

### From the farm to the home
Follow a common food, such as maize:

1. The farmer prepares land, plants, weeds and harvests.
2. The farmer may sell to a trader at the farm or at the market.
3. The trader transports the maize and sells it to families, to a mill, or to a shop.
4. A miller may grind it into flour.
5. A family buys the flour and cooks a meal.

The family depends on the farmer for food. The farmer depends on the family, through the trader, for income. The trader depends on both, and both depend on the trader to connect them. If any person in the chain stops, the others feel it.

### Other links around the farm
Farmers also depend on people who make or sell tools, on transporters, and sometimes on vets who treat animals. In a dry season they depend on people who can supply water or who will buy animals. Buyers in town depend on farmers even if they have never visited the farm.

Trade is not only food. A shopkeeper depends on customers. Customers depend on the shopkeeper for salt, soap, exercise books and medicines that the shop is allowed to sell. Trade with a neighbouring county means your county depends on people outside its boundary as well.

### Fair dependence
Interdependence works better when the exchange is fair. A buyer should pay the agreed price. A seller should give the amount and quality they promised. Cheating breaks the trust that trade needs. Social justice here means each person in the chain is treated fairly, including the farmer who did the long work of growing the crop.

Use a print or digital resource, such as a textbook photograph of a market, to name more links. Then draw your own chain for a food that families in your county actually eat. If you are not sure who sells it, ask at home and fill the chain afterwards.

## Key words
• trade — buying and selling goods and services
• farmer — a person who grows crops or keeps animals
• trader — a person who buys goods and sells them to others

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Put these in an order that shows interdependence: family cooks ugali, miller grinds maize, farmer harvests maize, trader buys the maize.

Working:
1. The crop starts with the farmer.
2. Then the trader, the miller and the family.

Answer: Farmer harvests maize, trader buys it, miller grinds it, family cooks ugali.

## Activity: A food chain of people
You will need: Textbook or a market photograph, Paper, Coloured pencils
1. Use a print or digital picture of trade to name the people you see.
2. Choose one food eaten in your county and list every person it passes through.
3. Draw them in order and write what each person needs from the next.
4. Share the chain and discuss what happens if the trader is missing.

## Practice
1. What is trade?
2. How does a farmer depend on a family that buys flour?
3. Give one way cheating harms interdependence in the market.

## Summary
• Farmers, traders, millers and families form a chain of need.
• Shops and trade with neighbouring counties are part of the same idea.
• Fair payment and honest goods keep the chain strong.

### Answers to practice
1. Buying and selling goods and services.
2. The family, through the trader or miller, provides the income the farmer needs.
3. It breaks trust, so people may refuse to trade or may be treated unfairly.

PAGE 4: Lesson 3: Hospitals and places of worship

LESSON 3: HOSPITALS AND PLACES OF WORSHIP
=========================================

## What you will learn
• Explain how people depend on a hospital and on the people who work there.
• Explain how people depend on one another at places of worship.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify ways in which people depend on each other in the county

## Introduction
When someone in the family is very sick, the home cannot always provide the care that is needed. The family turns to a hospital, and the hospital can only help because many workers depend on one another too.

## Notes
### The hospital
A hospital or a health centre is a place where sick and injured people are treated. Patients depend on doctors, nurses, laboratory workers and pharmacists. Those workers depend on one another: a doctor may need a laboratory result before choosing treatment, and a nurse carries out much of the daily care.

The hospital also depends on people the patient may never see. Cleaners keep wards safe. Cooks prepare food. Drivers bring supplies. Technicians look after equipment. County health workers may visit communities. Families depend on all of these people, and the workers depend on the community to use the hospital responsibly and to support it through the county's services.

Using a hospital well is part of interdependence. Go when you need care, follow the instructions you are given, wait your turn, and thank the people who help you. Do not crowd a room or demand to be seen before a more urgent patient.

### Places of worship
Places of worship include churches, mosques, temples and other places where people pray. They are part of interdependence in the county because people gather there not only to worship but also to support one another.

Members visit the sick, contribute food or money when a family is in need, teach children, and comfort people who are grieving. A person who is strong this year may be the person who needs help next year. Religious teachings in many communities tell people to care for neighbours. You can explain that importance without quoting a text you are not sure of: people at a place of worship promise to look after one another.

Leaders at these places depend on members to take part and to keep the compound clean and peaceful. Members depend on leaders to guide them fairly. Visitors of another faith should be treated with respect. Interdependence does not mean everyone worships in the same way. It means people in the county still need one another's kindness.

Add hospitals and places of worship to the class list of ways people depend on each other. Note the ones that serve your area, using names your teacher confirms.

## Key words
• patient — a person who is receiving care for an illness or injury
• place of worship — a church, mosque, temple or other place where people pray

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Name three groups of people a patient depends on in a hospital, including one group the patient may not meet.

Working:
1. Include people in the ward and people who support the hospital.

Answer: Any three, for example nurses, doctors, and cleaners or cooks.

### Example 2
Give one way members of a place of worship depend on each other outside the prayer time.

Working:
1. Think of help given to families.

Answer: They may visit the sick, share food, comfort a grieving family, or teach children.

## Activity: Who helps at the hospital and at worship
You will need: Two large sheets headed Hospital and Place of worship, Print or digital pictures if available
1. List the people who work in a hospital and say who depends on each of them.
2. List ways people support one another through a place of worship in your county.
3. Use a textbook or a digital resource to add any important role you missed.
4. Share the lists and correct any name of a local hospital only if the teacher confirms it.

## Practice
1. Why does a doctor sometimes depend on a laboratory worker?
2. Name one unseen hospital worker and what patients depend on them for.
3. How can people at a place of worship show interdependence?

## Summary
• A hospital works because many workers depend on one another.
• Patients depend on that whole team, not only on one person.
• Places of worship are communities where people support one another.

### Answers to practice
1. The doctor may need test results before choosing the right treatment.
2. Any one, for example cleaners for a safe ward, cooks for meals, or drivers for supplies.
3. By praying together and by helping one another, for example visiting the sick or sharing food with a family in need.

PAGE 5: Lesson 4: Benefits of depending on one another

LESSON 4: BENEFITS OF DEPENDING ON ONE ANOTHER
==============================================

## What you will learn
• Explain the benefits of interdependence in the county.
• Match each benefit to an example from trade, farming, health or worship.

Curriculum outcomes: b) explain the benefits of interdependence of people in the county

## Introduction
If every family tried to live without traders, nurses or neighbours, life would be harder and less safe. The benefits of interdependence are the good results that come when people support one another.

## Notes
A benefit is a good result. Interdependence in the county brings several benefits that you should be able to explain with an example, not only name.

### Needs are met
People get goods and services they cannot produce alone. A family gets food from farmers, treatment from a hospital, and learning from a school. Farmers get tools and buyers. This is the most direct benefit.

### Work is shared and skills grow
Because people specialise, they become good at their work. A nurse practises care. A trader learns how to store grain so that it does not spoil. The county gains many skills instead of everyone doing every job badly.

### Livelihoods
Interdependence creates work. The farmer's crop gives work to the trader, the transporter and the miller. A hospital employs cleaners and cooks as well as doctors. When people support local trade, they help those livelihoods.

### Peace and belonging
People who need one another have a reason to solve quarrels. Trade between communities, and help given at places of worship, pull people together. This is social cohesion: the feeling that we are one county even though we do different work and may worship in different ways. Social justice means the benefits should reach people fairly, not only those who are already comfortable.

### Help in hard times
In a dry season, a sickness, or after a flood, families get through because others share food, treatment and shelter. The person who gives help this year may need it next year. That is a reason to support one another before the hard time comes.

There is a limit to explain honestly. Depending on one another is not an excuse to sit idle and wait for neighbours to do your chores. Each person contributes what they can. Children contribute by learning, by doing their tasks at home, and by treating sellers, nurses and worshippers with respect.

Discuss in groups which benefit you have seen in your county. Use an example you know, and do not invent a story about a hospital or a market you cannot describe truthfully.

## Key words
• benefit — a good result
• livelihood — the work someone does to earn a living
• social cohesion — people living together in unity despite their differences

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A mill employs three workers because farmers sell maize there. Which benefit of interdependence is this?

Working:
1. People have jobs because of the links between farm and mill.

Answer: It creates livelihoods, or work.

### Example 2
Give one benefit of interdependence during a flood.

Working:
1. Think of needs people cannot meet alone.

Answer: Neighbours and services can share shelter, food or medical care.

## Activity: Match benefits to examples
You will need: Cards labelled with benefits, Blank cards for local examples
1. Write the benefits: needs met, skills, livelihoods, peace, help in hard times.
2. Each group adds a real example from the county for at least three benefits.
3. Explain the examples aloud and let other groups ask questions.
4. Discuss why supporting one another is fairer than leaving some people with no help.

## Practice
1. What is a benefit?
2. Explain one benefit of interdependence using farmers and families.
3. Why is interdependence not an excuse to do nothing?

## Summary
• Interdependence meets needs, builds skills and creates work.
• It also supports peace and help in hard times.
• Everyone, including learners, has something to contribute.

### Answers to practice
1. A good result.
2. Families get food they did not grow, and farmers earn a living from the crops they sell.
3. Each person should contribute what they can, including children doing their tasks and learning.

PAGE 6: Lesson 5: A chart of the benefits

LESSON 5: A CHART OF THE BENEFITS
=================================

## What you will learn
• Draw a chart that illustrates the benefits of interdependence.
• Present the chart so that another group can read it.

Curriculum outcomes: c) use chart to illustrate the benefits of interdependence people; b) explain the benefits of interdependence of people in the county

## Introduction
A long talk about interdependence is hard to remember. A chart puts the people, the links and the benefits where everyone can see them at once.

## Notes
A chart is an organised drawing or table. In this lesson the chart has one job: to illustrate the benefits of interdependence among people. Illustrate means a person who was not in your discussion can still understand the benefit from what you drew.

### Plan the chart
Use a title: "Benefits of interdependence in our county".

A clear layout has four columns:

- People: for example farmer and trader, nurse and patient, members of a place of worship
- How they depend on each other
- Benefit
- A small drawing

Four rows are enough: trade, farming, hospital, and a place of worship. You may add school if you have space. Keep the writing short. "Farmer sells maize; family gets food; farmer earns a living" is better than a crowded paragraph.

### Drawings
Use simple figures and symbols: a sack for trade, a hoe for farming, a red cross or a building with a cross or a crescent only if it truly matches the place you mean, and open hands for help. If your county has both churches and mosques, do not draw only one and pretend it is the whole story. You can draw two simple buildings and label them "places of worship".

Colour each benefit in the same colour every time it appears, and add a key. For example, green for "needs are met" and blue for "livelihoods". A key stops the reader guessing.

### Working with respect
Share the marker pens and the space on the paper. If you disagree about an example, check it against the class notes. Do not shout down a classmate. Social cohesion includes the way you make the chart, not only the words on it.

When the chart is finished, swap with another group. Their test of your work is whether they can explain one benefit without your help. If they cannot, add a label and try again. Display the charts in class.

## Key words
• chart — an organised table or drawing that shows information clearly
• illustrate — to show an idea so that someone else can understand it

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A chart says only "hospital — good". Why is that not enough, and what should be added?

Working:
1. The reader cannot see the link or the benefit.

Answer: Add the people, how they depend on each other, and a clear benefit, such as patients receive treatment and health workers have work.

## Activity: Draw the benefits chart
You will need: Manila paper, Marker pens, A ruler, Class notes on benefits
1. Rule a chart with columns for people, how they depend, the benefit, and a drawing.
2. Complete rows for trade, farming, hospital and places of worship.
3. Add a title, a key and simple drawings.
4. Swap charts and check whether another group can explain a benefit.
5. Display the chart and improve any label that was unclear.

## Practice
1. What is the title you should give this chart?
2. Why does the chart need a key?
3. What three things should a hospital row show?

## Summary
• A chart shows people, the link between them, and the benefit.
• Include trade, farming, hospitals and places of worship.
• Another group should be able to read the benefit without extra explanation.

### Answers to practice
1. Benefits of interdependence in our county
2. So that the reader knows what the colours or symbols mean.
3. The people, how they depend on each other, and the benefit.

PAGE 7: Lesson 6: Showing that we value interdependence

LESSON 6: SHOWING THAT WE VALUE INTERDEPENDENCE
===============================================

## What you will learn
• Role-play interdependence and recite a poem about its importance.
• Report what parents or guardians say about why people should support one another.

Curriculum outcomes: d) appreciate the interdependence of people in the County; b) explain the benefits of interdependence of people in the county

## Introduction
Understanding interdependence is useful when it changes how you act. A role-play, a poem and a conversation at home help you practise gratitude and fairness, not only repeat a definition.

## Notes
To appreciate interdependence is to be glad that people support one another and to play your part. You can show that appreciation in words and in behaviour.

### Role-play
In a role-play you act a short scene. Try one of these:

- A farmer and a trader agree a fair price for a sack of maize. A buyer then explains what the family will cook.
- A patient arrives at a hospital. A nurse, a cleaner and a doctor each say what they do and who needs them.
- At a place of worship, members plan how to take food to a sick neighbour.

Keep the scene kind and truthful. Do not mock a job, an illness or a religion. After the scene, the class names the benefit they saw.

### A poem
Reciting a poem builds the speaking skills you use in English, and it fixes the idea in your memory. Learn these lines or write your own:

The farmer grows the food we eat,
The trader brings it down the street.
The nurse is there when we are ill,
Neighbours help, and so we will.
I have a task that I can do.
Our county thrives when I help too.

Say it clearly, together, then let volunteers say it alone. Talk about the last two lines: appreciation includes your own contribution.

### Ask at home
Ask a parent or guardian why people in the county should support one another. Write their answer in two or three sentences and bring it back. Report it in your own words, and say thank you. Add any new benefit to the class chart if the class agrees it is true.

In daily life, appreciation looks ordinary. You greet the person who sells your family vegetables. You do not waste the food a farmer worked for. You wait your turn at a clinic. You help a classmate who is struggling. Those habits are interdependence in action.

## Key words
• role-play — acting a short scene to show a real situation
• appreciate — to value something and show it in what you say and do

## Worked examples

### Example 1
The last two lines of the poem say you have a task to do. Give one task a Grade 4 learner can do to support interdependence at school.

Working:
1. Choose a real, kind action.

Answer: Any one, for example helping a classmate, greeting the people who sell food, or not wasting food.

## Activity: Role-play and poem
You will need: The poem written on the board, Simple props such as a sack or a scarf, Notebooks for the home report
1. In groups, role-play one scene: market, hospital or place of worship.
2. The watching group names the people and the benefit.
3. Recite the poem together until the class can say it clearly.
4. At home, ask a parent or guardian why people should support one another, and report the answer next lesson.
5. Add one new true point to the benefits chart.

## Practice
1. What does it mean to appreciate interdependence?
2. Give one rule for a respectful role-play about a hospital.
3. Why should you report a parent's answer in your own words?
4. Name one daily habit that shows you value the farmer's work.

## Summary
• Role-play and a poem help us remember why people need one another.
• Families can add reasons to support each other in the county.
• Appreciation shows in fair, everyday habits.

### Answers to practice
1. To value the way people support one another and to play your own part.
2. Do not mock illness or a person's job. Show how the workers help the patient.
3. So that you show you understood it, and so that you can explain it to the class.
4. Not wasting food, or greeting and thanking the person who sells it.

REVISION QUIZ — 2.1 INTER-DEPENDENCE OF PEOPLE
========================================

Answer all the questions, then mark yourself on the Answers tab.

1. Interdependence means that people ___.
   A. never meet
   B. need one another
   C. all do the same job
   D. live without trade

2. Who depends on whom when a tailor buys maize from a farmer?

3. Which order best shows a food chain of people?
   A. Family, farmer, trader
   B. Farmer, trader, family
   C. Trader, farmer, empty shop
   D. Hospital, river, compass

4. A patient depends on nurses and doctors. Who else does the hospital depend on?
   A. Nobody
   B. Cleaners, cooks or drivers who support the hospital
   C. Only the weather
   D. Only monuments

5. How can members of a place of worship show interdependence?

6. Which is a benefit of interdependence?
   A. People get goods and services they cannot produce alone
   B. Everyone must farm
   C. Trade becomes impossible
   D. Hospitals close

7. A mill employs workers because farmers sell maize there. Which benefit is this?
   A. Livelihoods are created
   B. The rainy season ends
   C. Maps become unnecessary
   D. Specialising stops

8. Why should a benefits chart include how people depend, not only the word good?

9. Which columns make a clear interdependence chart?
   A. People, how they depend, benefit
   B. Only colours
   C. County boundaries and rainfall
   D. North, South, East, West

10. Which habit shows that you appreciate interdependence?
   A. Wasting food
   B. Mocking a nurse in a role-play
   C. Thanking the seller and not wasting food
   D. Refusing to help at home

11. What should you do with a parent's answer about supporting others?
   A. Ignore it
   B. Report it in your own words and add any true new point to the chart
   C. Pretend it is a county boundary
   D. Recite it as a monument
pages.answers:
ANSWERS — 2.1 INTER-DEPENDENCE OF PEOPLE
========================================

1. B. need one another
   Each person both needs others and is needed by them.

2. They depend on each other. The tailor needs food and the farmer needs a buyer.
   The need goes both ways.

3. B. Farmer, trader, family
   The farmer produces the food, the trader moves it, and the family uses it. A miller may come between trader and family.

4. B. Cleaners, cooks or drivers who support the hospital
   Many unseen workers keep a hospital going.

5. By supporting one another, for example visiting the sick or sharing food with a family in need.
   Places of worship are communities of mutual help as well as prayer.

6. A. People get goods and services they cannot produce alone
   Meeting needs we cannot meet alone is a main benefit.

7. A. Livelihoods are created
   Links between people create work.

8. So that a reader can see the link and the actual benefit.
   A chart illustrates the idea; a single vague word does not.

9. A. People, how they depend, benefit
   Those columns show the link and the good result.

10. C. Thanking the seller and not wasting food
   Appreciation includes fair, everyday actions.

11. B. Report it in your own words and add any true new point to the chart
   The home report is a source of reasons to value interdependence.

studyPages.body:
OVERVIEW
========

Interdependence means that people need one another. In your county, families depend on farmers and traders for food, on hospitals when they are sick, and on places of worship and neighbours for support. This sub-strand shows those links, the benefits they bring, and how to present them on a chart, in a role-play and in a poem.

## Strand 2.0: People and Population
Sub-strand 2.1: Inter-dependence of people
Suggested lessons: 6

## Learning outcomes
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) identify ways in which people depend on each other in the county
b) explain the benefits of interdependence of people in the county
c) use chart to illustrate the benefits of interdependence people
d) appreciate the interdependence of people in the County

## What this sub-strand covers
• trade
• farming
• hospital
• worship places

## Key inquiry questions
1. How do people in the county depend on each other?
2. Why should we support each other in the county?

## Core competencies
• Citizenship: Learners explain the benefits of interdependence of people in the county.
• Creativity and imagination: Learners role-play the interdependence of people in the county.

## Values
• Social justice: Learners discuss benefits of interdependence among people in the county

## Pertinent and contemporary issues
• Social cohesion: Learners identify ways in which people depend on each other in the county.
• Social cohesion: Learners respect others’ views/feelings as they work to create a chart on benefits of interdependence among people.

## Links to other learning areas
• English: Learners develop communication skills as they recite a poem about the importance of interdependence of people.
• Religious Education: Learners explain the importance of interdependence.

## Source
• KICD Grade 4 Social Studies Curriculum Design (Revised 2024) — Strand 2.0 People and Population, Sub-strand 2.1 Inter-dependence of people

studyPages.title: Lesson 1: People need one another
studyPages.body:
LESSON 1: PEOPLE NEED ONE ANOTHER
=================================

## What you will learn
• Explain the meaning of interdependence.
• Identify examples of people depending on each other in the county.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify ways in which people depend on each other in the county

## Introduction
Think about your breakfast. Someone grew the food, someone may have sold it, and someone at home cooked it. You depended on those people before the day even started.

## Notes
To depend on someone is to need them for something you cannot easily do alone. Interdependence means the need goes both ways. You need the farmer, and the farmer needs buyers so that the family can get money for soap, school costs and tools.

Nobody in a county grows all their own food, treats every illness, builds every house and teaches every child. People specialise. One person farms, another treats the sick, another teaches, another sells goods, another drives a vehicle. Specialising works only because people depend on each other.

### Examples close to you
Walk through one day and name the people you need:

- At home, you depend on the people who care for you. They depend on you to do your chores and to tell the truth.
- At school, you depend on your teachers. Teachers depend on learners to come ready to learn, and on parents to support the school.
- On the road, you depend on drivers to watch for walkers. Drivers depend on walkers to cross carefully.
- In the market, buyers and sellers depend on each other.

### In the county
The same pattern is larger. Villages depend on towns for some goods and services. Towns depend on villages for food. Neighbouring counties may trade with yours. When a hospital in one sub-county serves families from another, those families and that hospital are interdependent.

Brainstorm a list under the heading "People we need in our county". Keep the list for the next lessons, which look closely at trade, farming, hospitals and places of worship. Those four are important ways interdependence shows itself, but they are not the only ways.

A person who says "I need nobody" still uses roads others built, food others grew and a language others taught. Seeing the links is the first step to appreciating them.

## Key words
• depend — to need someone or something
• interdependence — people needing one another, so that each person both gives and receives help
• specialise — to do one kind of work that others rely on

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A tailor sews uniforms and buys maize from a farmer. Who depends on whom?

Working:
1. The farmer needs the tailor's payment, which comes because people need uniforms.
2. The tailor needs the farmer's maize for food.

Answer: They depend on each other. The tailor needs food, and the farmer needs buyers.

## Activity: Brainstorm who we need
You will need: Manila paper, Marker pens
1. In groups, brainstorm ways people in the county depend on each other.
2. Write each idea as "The ___ depends on the ___ for ___."
3. Read the list to the class and add ideas from other groups.
4. Underline any examples about trade, farming, a hospital or a place of worship.

## Practice
1. What does interdependence mean?
2. Give one way learners and teachers depend on each other.
3. Why does specialising make interdependence necessary?

## Summary
• Interdependence means people need one another.
• A single day shows many people you depend on.
• Trade, farming, hospitals and places of worship are important examples in the county.

### Answers to practice
1. People need one another, so that each person both gives help and receives help.
2. Learners need teachers to learn, and teachers need learners to come ready to learn.
3. When each person does one kind of work, they must rely on other people for the rest of what they need.

studyPages.title: Lesson 2: Trade and farming
studyPages.body:
LESSON 2: TRADE AND FARMING
===========================

## What you will learn
• Describe how farmers, traders and buyers depend on one another.
• Trace one food from the farm to the home.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify ways in which people depend on each other in the county

## Introduction
A market day is a picture of interdependence. Sacks of grain, vegetables, fish or milk arrive because farmers and traders need the people who have come to buy.

## Notes
Trade is the buying and selling of goods and services. Farming is the growing of crops and the keeping of animals. The two activities lock together.

### From the farm to the home
Follow a common food, such as maize:

1. The farmer prepares land, plants, weeds and harvests.
2. The farmer may sell to a trader at the farm or at the market.
3. The trader transports the maize and sells it to families, to a mill, or to a shop.
4. A miller may grind it into flour.
5. A family buys the flour and cooks a meal.

The family depends on the farmer for food. The farmer depends on the family, through the trader, for income. The trader depends on both, and both depend on the trader to connect them. If any person in the chain stops, the others feel it.

### Other links around the farm
Farmers also depend on people who make or sell tools, on transporters, and sometimes on vets who treat animals. In a dry season they depend on people who can supply water or who will buy animals. Buyers in town depend on farmers even if they have never visited the farm.

Trade is not only food. A shopkeeper depends on customers. Customers depend on the shopkeeper for salt, soap, exercise books and medicines that the shop is allowed to sell. Trade with a neighbouring county means your county depends on people outside its boundary as well.

### Fair dependence
Interdependence works better when the exchange is fair. A buyer should pay the agreed price. A seller should give the amount and quality they promised. Cheating breaks the trust that trade needs. Social justice here means each person in the chain is treated fairly, including the farmer who did the long work of growing the crop.

Use a print or digital resource, such as a textbook photograph of a market, to name more links. Then draw your own chain for a food that families in your county actually eat. If you are not sure who sells it, ask at home and fill the chain afterwards.

## Key words
• trade — buying and selling goods and services
• farmer — a person who grows crops or keeps animals
• trader — a person who buys goods and sells them to others

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Put these in an order that shows interdependence: family cooks ugali, miller grinds maize, farmer harvests maize, trader buys the maize.

Working:
1. The crop starts with the farmer.
2. Then the trader, the miller and the family.

Answer: Farmer harvests maize, trader buys it, miller grinds it, family cooks ugali.

## Activity: A food chain of people
You will need: Textbook or a market photograph, Paper, Coloured pencils
1. Use a print or digital picture of trade to name the people you see.
2. Choose one food eaten in your county and list every person it passes through.
3. Draw them in order and write what each person needs from the next.
4. Share the chain and discuss what happens if the trader is missing.

## Practice
1. What is trade?
2. How does a farmer depend on a family that buys flour?
3. Give one way cheating harms interdependence in the market.

## Summary
• Farmers, traders, millers and families form a chain of need.
• Shops and trade with neighbouring counties are part of the same idea.
• Fair payment and honest goods keep the chain strong.

### Answers to practice
1. Buying and selling goods and services.
2. The family, through the trader or miller, provides the income the farmer needs.
3. It breaks trust, so people may refuse to trade or may be treated unfairly.

studyPages.title: Lesson 3: Hospitals and places of worship
studyPages.body:
LESSON 3: HOSPITALS AND PLACES OF WORSHIP
=========================================

## What you will learn
• Explain how people depend on a hospital and on the people who work there.
• Explain how people depend on one another at places of worship.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify ways in which people depend on each other in the county

## Introduction
When someone in the family is very sick, the home cannot always provide the care that is needed. The family turns to a hospital, and the hospital can only help because many workers depend on one another too.

## Notes
### The hospital
A hospital or a health centre is a place where sick and injured people are treated. Patients depend on doctors, nurses, laboratory workers and pharmacists. Those workers depend on one another: a doctor may need a laboratory result before choosing treatment, and a nurse carries out much of the daily care.

The hospital also depends on people the patient may never see. Cleaners keep wards safe. Cooks prepare food. Drivers bring supplies. Technicians look after equipment. County health workers may visit communities. Families depend on all of these people, and the workers depend on the community to use the hospital responsibly and to support it through the county's services.

Using a hospital well is part of interdependence. Go when you need care, follow the instructions you are given, wait your turn, and thank the people who help you. Do not crowd a room or demand to be seen before a more urgent patient.

### Places of worship
Places of worship include churches, mosques, temples and other places where people pray. They are part of interdependence in the county because people gather there not only to worship but also to support one another.

Members visit the sick, contribute food or money when a family is in need, teach children, and comfort people who are grieving. A person who is strong this year may be the person who needs help next year. Religious teachings in many communities tell people to care for neighbours. You can explain that importance without quoting a text you are not sure of: people at a place of worship promise to look after one another.

Leaders at these places depend on members to take part and to keep the compound clean and peaceful. Members depend on leaders to guide them fairly. Visitors of another faith should be treated with respect. Interdependence does not mean everyone worships in the same way. It means people in the county still need one another's kindness.

Add hospitals and places of worship to the class list of ways people depend on each other. Note the ones that serve your area, using names your teacher confirms.

## Key words
• patient — a person who is receiving care for an illness or injury
• place of worship — a church, mosque, temple or other place where people pray

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Name three groups of people a patient depends on in a hospital, including one group the patient may not meet.

Working:
1. Include people in the ward and people who support the hospital.

Answer: Any three, for example nurses, doctors, and cleaners or cooks.

### Example 2
Give one way members of a place of worship depend on each other outside the prayer time.

Working:
1. Think of help given to families.

Answer: They may visit the sick, share food, comfort a grieving family, or teach children.

## Activity: Who helps at the hospital and at worship
You will need: Two large sheets headed Hospital and Place of worship, Print or digital pictures if available
1. List the people who work in a hospital and say who depends on each of them.
2. List ways people support one another through a place of worship in your county.
3. Use a textbook or a digital resource to add any important role you missed.
4. Share the lists and correct any name of a local hospital only if the teacher confirms it.

## Practice
1. Why does a doctor sometimes depend on a laboratory worker?
2. Name one unseen hospital worker and what patients depend on them for.
3. How can people at a place of worship show interdependence?

## Summary
• A hospital works because many workers depend on one another.
• Patients depend on that whole team, not only on one person.
• Places of worship are communities where people support one another.

### Answers to practice
1. The doctor may need test results before choosing the right treatment.
2. Any one, for example cleaners for a safe ward, cooks for meals, or drivers for supplies.
3. By praying together and by helping one another, for example visiting the sick or sharing food with a family in need.

studyPages.title: Lesson 4: Benefits of depending on one another
studyPages.body:
LESSON 4: BENEFITS OF DEPENDING ON ONE ANOTHER
==============================================

## What you will learn
• Explain the benefits of interdependence in the county.
• Match each benefit to an example from trade, farming, health or worship.

Curriculum outcomes: b) explain the benefits of interdependence of people in the county

## Introduction
If every family tried to live without traders, nurses or neighbours, life would be harder and less safe. The benefits of interdependence are the good results that come when people support one another.

## Notes
A benefit is a good result. Interdependence in the county brings several benefits that you should be able to explain with an example, not only name.

### Needs are met
People get goods and services they cannot produce alone. A family gets food from farmers, treatment from a hospital, and learning from a school. Farmers get tools and buyers. This is the most direct benefit.

### Work is shared and skills grow
Because people specialise, they become good at their work. A nurse practises care. A trader learns how to store grain so that it does not spoil. The county gains many skills instead of everyone doing every job badly.

### Livelihoods
Interdependence creates work. The farmer's crop gives work to the trader, the transporter and the miller. A hospital employs cleaners and cooks as well as doctors. When people support local trade, they help those livelihoods.

### Peace and belonging
People who need one another have a reason to solve quarrels. Trade between communities, and help given at places of worship, pull people together. This is social cohesion: the feeling that we are one county even though we do different work and may worship in different ways. Social justice means the benefits should reach people fairly, not only those who are already comfortable.

### Help in hard times
In a dry season, a sickness, or after a flood, families get through because others share food, treatment and shelter. The person who gives help this year may need it next year. That is a reason to support one another before the hard time comes.

There is a limit to explain honestly. Depending on one another is not an excuse to sit idle and wait for neighbours to do your chores. Each person contributes what they can. Children contribute by learning, by doing their tasks at home, and by treating sellers, nurses and worshippers with respect.

Discuss in groups which benefit you have seen in your county. Use an example you know, and do not invent a story about a hospital or a market you cannot describe truthfully.

## Key words
• benefit — a good result
• livelihood — the work someone does to earn a living
• social cohesion — people living together in unity despite their differences

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A mill employs three workers because farmers sell maize there. Which benefit of interdependence is this?

Working:
1. People have jobs because of the links between farm and mill.

Answer: It creates livelihoods, or work.

### Example 2
Give one benefit of interdependence during a flood.

Working:
1. Think of needs people cannot meet alone.

Answer: Neighbours and services can share shelter, food or medical care.

## Activity: Match benefits to examples
You will need: Cards labelled with benefits, Blank cards for local examples
1. Write the benefits: needs met, skills, livelihoods, peace, help in hard times.
2. Each group adds a real example from the county for at least three benefits.
3. Explain the examples aloud and let other groups ask questions.
4. Discuss why supporting one another is fairer than leaving some people with no help.

## Practice
1. What is a benefit?
2. Explain one benefit of interdependence using farmers and families.
3. Why is interdependence not an excuse to do nothing?

## Summary
• Interdependence meets needs, builds skills and creates work.
• It also supports peace and help in hard times.
• Everyone, including learners, has something to contribute.

### Answers to practice
1. A good result.
2. Families get food they did not grow, and farmers earn a living from the crops they sell.
3. Each person should contribute what they can, including children doing their tasks and learning.

studyPages.title: Lesson 5: A chart of the benefits
studyPages.body:
LESSON 5: A CHART OF THE BENEFITS
=================================

## What you will learn
• Draw a chart that illustrates the benefits of interdependence.
• Present the chart so that another group can read it.

Curriculum outcomes: c) use chart to illustrate the benefits of interdependence people; b) explain the benefits of interdependence of people in the county

## Introduction
A long talk about interdependence is hard to remember. A chart puts the people, the links and the benefits where everyone can see them at once.

## Notes
A chart is an organised drawing or table. In this lesson the chart has one job: to illustrate the benefits of interdependence among people. Illustrate means a person who was not in your discussion can still understand the benefit from what you drew.

### Plan the chart
Use a title: "Benefits of interdependence in our county".

A clear layout has four columns:

- People: for example farmer and trader, nurse and patient, members of a place of worship
- How they depend on each other
- Benefit
- A small drawing

Four rows are enough: trade, farming, hospital, and a place of worship. You may add school if you have space. Keep the writing short. "Farmer sells maize; family gets food; farmer earns a living" is better than a crowded paragraph.

### Drawings
Use simple figures and symbols: a sack for trade, a hoe for farming, a red cross or a building with a cross or a crescent only if it truly matches the place you mean, and open hands for help. If your county has both churches and mosques, do not draw only one and pretend it is the whole story. You can draw two simple buildings and label them "places of worship".

Colour each benefit in the same colour every time it appears, and add a key. For example, green for "needs are met" and blue for "livelihoods". A key stops the reader guessing.

### Working with respect
Share the marker pens and the space on the paper. If you disagree about an example, check it against the class notes. Do not shout down a classmate. Social cohesion includes the way you make the chart, not only the words on it.

When the chart is finished, swap with another group. Their test of your work is whether they can explain one benefit without your help. If they cannot, add a label and try again. Display the charts in class.

## Key words
• chart — an organised table or drawing that shows information clearly
• illustrate — to show an idea so that someone else can understand it

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A chart says only "hospital — good". Why is that not enough, and what should be added?

Working:
1. The reader cannot see the link or the benefit.

Answer: Add the people, how they depend on each other, and a clear benefit, such as patients receive treatment and health workers have work.

## Activity: Draw the benefits chart
You will need: Manila paper, Marker pens, A ruler, Class notes on benefits
1. Rule a chart with columns for people, how they depend, the benefit, and a drawing.
2. Complete rows for trade, farming, hospital and places of worship.
3. Add a title, a key and simple drawings.
4. Swap charts and check whether another group can explain a benefit.
5. Display the chart and improve any label that was unclear.

## Practice
1. What is the title you should give this chart?
2. Why does the chart need a key?
3. What three things should a hospital row show?

## Summary
• A chart shows people, the link between them, and the benefit.
• Include trade, farming, hospitals and places of worship.
• Another group should be able to read the benefit without extra explanation.

### Answers to practice
1. Benefits of interdependence in our county
2. So that the reader knows what the colours or symbols mean.
3. The people, how they depend on each other, and the benefit.

studyPages.title: Lesson 6: Showing that we value interdependence
studyPages.body:
LESSON 6: SHOWING THAT WE VALUE INTERDEPENDENCE
===============================================

## What you will learn
• Role-play interdependence and recite a poem about its importance.
• Report what parents or guardians say about why people should support one another.

Curriculum outcomes: d) appreciate the interdependence of people in the County; b) explain the benefits of interdependence of people in the county

## Introduction
Understanding interdependence is useful when it changes how you act. A role-play, a poem and a conversation at home help you practise gratitude and fairness, not only repeat a definition.

## Notes
To appreciate interdependence is to be glad that people support one another and to play your part. You can show that appreciation in words and in behaviour.

### Role-play
In a role-play you act a short scene. Try one of these:

- A farmer and a trader agree a fair price for a sack of maize. A buyer then explains what the family will cook.
- A patient arrives at a hospital. A nurse, a cleaner and a doctor each say what they do and who needs them.
- At a place of worship, members plan how to take food to a sick neighbour.

Keep the scene kind and truthful. Do not mock a job, an illness or a religion. After the scene, the class names the benefit they saw.

### A poem
Reciting a poem builds the speaking skills you use in English, and it fixes the idea in your memory. Learn these lines or write your own:

The farmer grows the food we eat,
The trader brings it down the street.
The nurse is there when we are ill,
Neighbours help, and so we will.
I have a task that I can do.
Our county thrives when I help too.

Say it clearly, together, then let volunteers say it alone. Talk about the last two lines: appreciation includes your own contribution.

### Ask at home
Ask a parent or guardian why people in the county should support one another. Write their answer in two or three sentences and bring it back. Report it in your own words, and say thank you. Add any new benefit to the class chart if the class agrees it is true.

In daily life, appreciation looks ordinary. You greet the person who sells your family vegetables. You do not waste the food a farmer worked for. You wait your turn at a clinic. You help a classmate who is struggling. Those habits are interdependence in action.

## Key words
• role-play — acting a short scene to show a real situation
• appreciate — to value something and show it in what you say and do

## Worked examples

### Example 1
The last two lines of the poem say you have a task to do. Give one task a Grade 4 learner can do to support interdependence at school.

Working:
1. Choose a real, kind action.

Answer: Any one, for example helping a classmate, greeting the people who sell food, or not wasting food.

## Activity: Role-play and poem
You will need: The poem written on the board, Simple props such as a sack or a scarf, Notebooks for the home report
1. In groups, role-play one scene: market, hospital or place of worship.
2. The watching group names the people and the benefit.
3. Recite the poem together until the class can say it clearly.
4. At home, ask a parent or guardian why people should support one another, and report the answer next lesson.
5. Add one new true point to the benefits chart.

## Practice
1. What does it mean to appreciate interdependence?
2. Give one rule for a respectful role-play about a hospital.
3. Why should you report a parent's answer in your own words?
4. Name one daily habit that shows you value the farmer's work.

## Summary
• Role-play and a poem help us remember why people need one another.
• Families can add reasons to support each other in the county.
• Appreciation shows in fair, everyday habits.

### Answers to practice
1. To value the way people support one another and to play your own part.
2. Do not mock illness or a person's job. Show how the workers help the patient.
3. So that you show you understood it, and so that you can explain it to the class.
4. Not wasting food, or greeting and thanking the person who sells it.

questions.question: Interdependence means that people ___.
questions.explanation: Each person both needs others and is needed by them.

questions.question: Who depends on whom when a tailor buys maize from a farmer?
questions.answer: They depend on each other. The tailor needs food and the farmer needs a buyer.

questions.question: Which order best shows a food chain of people?
questions.explanation: The farmer produces the food, the trader moves it, and the family uses it. A miller may come between trader and family.

questions.question: A patient depends on nurses and doctors. Who else does the hospital depend on?
options: Cleaners, cooks or drivers who support the hospital
questions.explanation: Many unseen workers keep a hospital going.

questions.question: How can members of a place of worship show interdependence?
questions.answer: By supporting one another, for example visiting the sick or sharing food with a family in need.
questions.explanation: Places of worship are communities of mutual help as well as prayer.

questions.question: Which is a benefit of interdependence?
options: People get goods and services they cannot produce alone
questions.explanation: Meeting needs we cannot meet alone is a main benefit.

questions.question: A mill employs workers because farmers sell maize there. Which benefit is this?
Why should a benefits chart include how people depend, not only the word good?
questions.answer: So that a reader can see the link and the actual benefit.
questions.explanation: A chart illustrates the idea; a single vague word does not.

questions.question: Which columns make a clear interdependence chart?
questions.explanation: Those columns show the link and the good result.

questions.question: Which habit shows that you appreciate interdependence?
options: Mocking a nurse in a role-play
Thanking the seller and not wasting food

questions.question: What should you do with a parent's answer about supporting others?
options: Report it in your own words and add any true new point to the chart
Pretend it is a county boundary
questions.explanation: The home report is a source of reasons to value interdependence.
